opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a great question, and it gets at what motivates a lot of my research on open-endedness.

The standard recipe in reinforcement learning is: you have an environment, you write down a reward function, and you optimize a policy to maximize that reward. That works remarkably well when the problem is well specified. We've seen it with Go, with Atari, and more recently with fine-tuning language models on tasks where you can verify the answer, like math or code. But the system you get out at the end can only be as good, and as general, as the task you handed it. You've essentially baked the ceiling into the problem definition.

There are a few issues with that. One is that specifying rewards is really hard. Anything you can write down is a proxy for what you actually want, and powerful optimizers are very good at finding the gap between the proxy and the intent. That's reward hacking. The more capable the agent, the more creatively it exploits misspecification.

The second, more fundamental issue is that general capability isn't really one task. If you want a system that keeps getting better, that discovers new skills and new knowledge, you'd need an endless stream of new, interesting problems at just the right difficulty. No human team can hand-design that. At some point the bottleneck stops being the learning algorithm and becomes the supply of good problems and environments.

That's why I'm excited about open-ended systems: systems that generate their own tasks, their own curricula, and in some sense their own goals, and keep producing novel, learnable artifacts forever. If you look at biological evolution or human culture and science, there was never a single fixed reward function. There's a process that keeps creating new niches, new problems, and new stepping stones, and capabilities emerge from that. Often the stepping stones toward something impressive look nothing like the final goal, so if you optimize directly for the objective you'd never find them.

So I'd say reward plus RL is a really powerful component, and I don't think it goes away. But on its own, with a human-defined objective and a fixed environment, it's not sufficient. You need something on top that keeps generating novelty and learnability. And foundation models are interesting here, because they bring a notion of what humans find interesting, which can help drive that open-ended process in directions that are actually meaningful to us.

r001.rationale: The response says rewards are hard to specify and fixed objectives limit general capability, but it does not state that most interesting domains lack a suitable reward function.

r002.rationale: It advocates open-ended systems that generate tasks and novelty, but does not clearly describe curiosity-driven autonomous exploration specifically in domains without a suitable reward function.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is that reinforcement learning, as a framework, is actually quite general. If you can write down a reward function, and you have an environment, then in principle you can learn almost anything. The problem is the "if you can write down a reward function" part, and the "you have an environment" part. Those two assumptions hide most of the difficulty.

When we design a reward function, we're essentially encoding our own understanding of the task. We're saying, this is what good behavior looks like, go find it. And that works beautifully for things like Go or Atari, where the objective is crisp and the environment is fixed. But as soon as you move to anything resembling the real world, the reward is underspecified, it's sparse, it's easy to game, and the agent will happily find some degenerate solution that maximizes the number without doing anything we'd recognize as intelligent. Every RL researcher has a story about reward hacking. That's not a bug in the agent, it's a symptom of the fact that we're bottlenecked on humans specifying what we want.

And the environment side is maybe even more important. If I train an agent in a single environment, I get an agent that's good at that environment. The distribution of experiences it sees is bounded by what I built. Generality doesn't come from a clever algorithm sitting on top of a narrow world. It comes from being exposed to a wide, diverse, ever-changing distribution of challenges. If you look at where human intelligence came from, nobody wrote down a reward function for evolution. There was an open-ended process where the problems themselves kept changing, organisms adapted, that created new problems, and so on. The complexity emerged from the dynamics of the process, not from a designer.

So my view is that if we want generally capable agents, we need to stop thinking of ourselves as the ones who hand-design every task and every objective, and instead build systems that generate their own curricula. Things like unsupervised environment design, where you have a second process that proposes environments at the frontier of what the agent can currently do, so it's always being pushed just beyond its competence. Or more broadly, open-ended learning, where the set of problems grows alongside the agent's abilities. In those settings, reward functions and RL are still there, they're the learning mechanism inside the loop, but they're not the thing that produces generality. The generality comes from the open-ended search over what to learn next.

The other piece I'd add is that we now have models trained on enormous amounts of human data that already encode a lot about the world. That changes the picture, because the environment and the task designer can themselves be driven by these models. But even there, I think the lesson holds. Scaling a fixed objective on a fixed distribution gets you to a plateau. Getting past that plateau requires a process that keeps discovering new things worth learning, and that's fundamentally not something you capture by writing down a single reward.

r001.rationale: The response says that real-world rewards are underspecified, sparse, and easy to game, and that human specification is the bottleneck—communicating that many interesting domains lack a suitable reward for general learning.

r002.rationale: It advocates open-ended learning and self-generated curricula, but does not clearly call for curiosity-driven autonomous exploration when a suitable reward function is unavailable.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is an important part of the picture, but it leaves a fundamental question unanswered: where do the tasks and rewards come from? If we define a reward function for a particular task, we can train an agent to become very good at that task. But that doesn’t necessarily give us an agent that can handle a new situation or work out what’s worth learning next.

And specifying the reward is itself difficult. We often know roughly what behavior we want, but expressing that as a scalar signal is much harder. The agent may find a way to maximize that signal that doesn’t correspond to what we intended.

For general capability, I think we need to look beyond optimizing a fixed objective in a fixed environment. We need systems that encounter—and perhaps help generate—new challenges, building on what they’ve already learned. That’s what makes open-ended learning interesting: the question becomes not just how to solve a task, but how to sustain a process that keeps producing useful new skills. Reinforcement learning can drive that process, but a reward function alone doesn’t tell us how to organize it.

r001.rationale: It says defining rewards is difficult and fixed rewards may not generalize, but does not state that most interesting domains lack a suitable reward function.

r002.rationale: It discusses encountering or generating new challenges and open-ended learning, but does not clearly advocate curiosity-driven autonomous exploration where suitable rewards are unavailable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is an important part of the picture, but it doesn’t by itself tell us where the problems worth solving come from. Typically, we define an environment and a reward function, and then train an agent to maximize that reward. You can get very impressive performance, but often it’s performance on precisely the task you specified. That doesn’t necessarily give you an agent that can deal with something fundamentally new.

The difficulty is that we can’t anticipate every situation a generally capable system will encounter and write down the right reward for each one. Even when we can specify a reward, it can be a poor proxy for what we actually want. The agent may find a way to maximize it that completely misses our intention.

So I’m interested in how we get systems that keep discovering new challenges and acquiring skills without us specifying every task in advance. That means thinking about exploration, curricula, and environments that can become more complex as the agent becomes more capable. Reinforcement learning can be the mechanism for learning within that process, but the reward maximization objective alone doesn’t provide that open-ended process.

r001.rationale: It says rewards can be hard to specify or may be poor proxies, but does not state that most interesting domains lack a suitable reward function.

r002.rationale: It advocates ongoing discovery and exploration without pre-specified tasks, but does not specifically advocate curiosity-driven exploration in domains where a suitable reward function is unavailable.
